B United States / Europe ｜ 1987

Historical event · story Black Monday market shock unfolded in United States / Europe during 1987. The mid-1980s equity boom had lifted valuations while computer-assisted trading and index futures created new links between cash and derivatives markets. Investors also worried about interest rates, currency tensions, and U.S. trade deficits. On Monday, 19 October 1987, stock markets around the world plunged. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6 percent, while European and Asian markets also suffered extraordinary declines. Trading systems struggled with order volume and price delays. The shock traveled through markets faster than many institutions could process information. Selling strategies that appeared reasonable individually interacted with one another, creating feedback at the exact moment liquidity was disappearing. Central banks emphasized liquidity, exchanges and regulators studied the event, and U.S. markets later adopted coordinated circuit breakers. Despite the severity of the one-day fall, the real economy did not enter a depression comparable to the 1930s. The event changed operational planning for market stress. It showed that a sudden financial shock can be survivable if payments, funding, and market infrastructure remain functioning, but it also revealed the need to prepare systems for volume far beyond ordinary conditions. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. B United States ｜ 1988 onward

Historical event · story Trading halts and market-wide circuit breakers unfolded in United States during 1988 onward. The 1987 crash showed that modern exchanges could experience price moves and order volumes so fast that participants lost confidence in quoted prices and trading systems. Regulators sought mechanisms that could create short pauses during extreme moves. U.S. exchanges introduced coordinated market-wide circuit breakers, later revised many times. Under current-style systems, specified declines in broad indexes can trigger temporary trading halts, with thresholds and timing rules designed to slow the market during extraordinary volatility. The economic purpose is to keep still briefly, allowing orders, information, and operational systems to catch up. A halt trades some immediacy for a chance to reduce mechanical disorder, especially when rapid feedback is overwhelming normal price discovery. Circuit breakers have been activated during later crises, including the market turmoil of March 2020. They do not determine the correct price or prevent losses; after the pause, trading resumes and prices can continue to move. Debate continues over whether halts calm markets or simply delay trading. Their existence nonetheless reflects an institutional judgment that continuous trading is not always the highest priority when market mechanics themselves are under stress. B European Community / European Union ｜ 1986–1993

Historical event · story European Single Market unfolded in European Community / European Union during 1986–1993. Postwar European integration had reduced tariffs, but many national rules, technical standards, border procedures, and restrictions on services and capital still divided markets. Businesses faced costs when operating across member states. The Single European Act of 1986 set a program to complete an internal market by the end of 1992. Hundreds of measures addressed product standards, public procurement, financial services, capital movements, professional rules, and border procedures. The project was gradual by design. Rather than one treaty instantly creating a unified economy, legal barriers were identified and removed in stages, while common standards and mutual recognition provided ways for national systems to interoperate. The single market formally began in 1993 and continued to deepen through later legislation and court decisions. It expanded cross-border trade and investment, although national differences and regulatory disputes remained. The result became one of the world’s largest integrated markets, but it has never been “finished” in every sector. Its history shows how economic integration can advance through many small, coordinated changes whose cumulative effect is larger than any single reform. B United States ｜ 2000–2009

Historical event · story AOL–Time Warner merger unfolded in United States during 2000–2009. At the height of the dot-com boom, America Online had a highly valued internet subscription business and an enormous stock-market capitalization. Time Warner owned major media, publishing, cable, and entertainment assets. In January 2000 the companies announced a stock merger valued at roughly $165 billion, presenting the deal as a combination of new internet distribution with established content. The transaction closed in 2001, just as the technology market was collapsing and broadband was beginning to weaken AOL’s dial-up model. The merger joined businesses with very different economics at a moment when one partner’s market valuation reflected exceptional expectations. The legal marriage was completed, but the strategic fit and relative bargaining positions changed soon afterward. The expected synergies proved difficult to realize. The combined company recorded enormous goodwill impairments, management conflicts became public, and AOL’s importance declined. Time Warner later separated AOL in 2009. The case became one of the most cited merger disappointments in corporate history. It shows that combining assets does not guarantee shared value when technology, valuation, culture, and cash-flow trends are moving in different directions. B United States ｜ 1920s

Historical event · story The Roaring Twenties credit boom unfolded in United States during 1920s. After the First World War, U.S. industry benefited from mass production, electrification, automobiles, consumer appliances, and rising productivity. Household installment credit and expanding securities markets helped more people buy goods and financial assets. Businesses invested, advertising expanded, and equity prices rose strongly in the second half of the decade. Brokers offered margin loans that allowed investors to buy shares with borrowed money. Prosperity was real in many sectors, but agriculture and some regions remained weak. The 1920s demonstrate how abundance can produce both genuine capacity and overconfidence. When incomes, technology, and asset prices rise together, investors may treat favorable conditions as permanent and increase leverage accordingly. The boom ended with the 1929 market crash and the deeper economic collapse that followed. The Depression cannot be explained by stock speculation alone, but the contrast between apparent abundance and subsequent contraction shaped public memory. Much of the era’s productive innovation survived the crash, while many financial valuations did not. The history therefore separates economic abundance from the assumption that every asset price observed during prosperous years is sustainable. B London / Europe / United States ｜ 1950s–1980s

Historical event · story The Eurodollar market unfolded in London / Europe / United States during 1950s–1980s. After the Second World War, U.S. dollars accumulated outside the United States through trade, aid, military spending, and reserve holdings. Banks in London and other centers began accepting dollar deposits and making dollar loans beyond the direct boundaries of U.S. domestic banking regulation. The Eurodollar market expanded rapidly in the 1960s and 1970s. International banks used offshore dollar deposits to finance trade, corporations, governments, and other banks. London’s time zone, legal system, and financial expertise helped it become a major center. The “traveler” was the dollar itself: a national currency became widely deposited and lent abroad, taking on financial life far from its issuing country. Banks and borrowers used the same unit of account without moving the activity back onshore. The market increased the global mobility of dollar credit and contributed to modern international banking. It also complicated monetary control because dollar liabilities could grow outside U.S. domestic reserve requirements. Eurocurrency markets later became integrated into a broader global banking system. The episode shows how finance follows demand across borders and how money can remain connected to its home central bank while circulating through institutions governed by different jurisdictions. B United States / Europe ｜ 1950s–1980s

Historical event · story The spread of credit cards unfolded in United States / Europe during 1950s–1980s. Consumer credit existed long before modern cards, but postwar growth in travel, retail, and banking created demand for a portable payment method that could be accepted by many unrelated merchants. Diners Club introduced a broad travel-and-entertainment charge card in 1950. BankAmericard launched in 1958 and evolved into Visa; Master Charge, later Mastercard, developed through a bank association. Standardized networks connected issuing banks, merchants, processors, and cardholders. The system expanded gently rather than through a single public mandate. Each additional cardholder made acceptance more valuable to merchants, and each additional merchant made the card more useful to consumers, creating a network effect. Cards spread across the United States and Europe, eventually becoming major payment and borrowing tools. They increased convenience and merchant sales but also created revolving debt, fees, fraud risks, and complex interchange economics. Later technologies moved cards online and into mobile wallets, but the underlying network logic remained. The history shows how a financial product can penetrate daily life by reducing transaction friction one merchant and one household at a time. B United States / Western Europe ｜ 1950s–1960s

Historical event · story Postwar consumer credit and mass consumption unfolded in United States / Western Europe during 1950s–1960s. After the Second World War, rising incomes, household formation, suburbanization, and new consumer goods created strong demand for cars, appliances, furniture, and housing. Many purchases were too large to fund from one paycheck. Banks, finance companies, retailers, and mortgage lenders expanded consumer credit. Installment loans allowed households to spread payments over time, while standardized underwriting and mass marketing made credit more widely available than before the war. Credit created immediate enjoyment by bringing future income into present consumption. The arrangement worked when repayment schedules fit household cash flow; it became harmful when borrowing costs or debt burdens exceeded the borrower’s capacity. Consumer spending supported rapid economic growth, and ownership of durable goods rose. At the same time, households became more exposed to interest costs and income shocks, and access to favorable credit remained unequal across race and neighborhood. The postwar credit boom helped define modern consumer economies in the United States and Western Europe. It also established a lasting tension in personal finance: borrowing can smooth consumption and build assets, but it can also convert short-term satisfaction into long-term obligations. Historical event · story Deregulation and electronic trading disperse market access unfolded in United States / Europe during 1970s–2000s. Securities markets were once concentrated in physical trading floors, fixed commission structures, and relatively small groups of exchange members. Rising institutional investment, computing, and telecommunications gradually weakened the need for every transaction to occur in one room. The United States ended fixed brokerage commissions in 1975, London’s Big Bang reshaped its market in 1986, and electronic communication networks later allowed orders to match outside traditional floors. Online brokerage in the 1990s brought direct market access to millions of households. Dispersion changed where liquidity lived. Instead of one visible crowd, orders could be divided across venues and routed by algorithms. This lowered some costs but made the overall market structure less intuitive to ordinary investors. Trading became faster, cheaper, and more geographically dispersed. Traditional exchanges adapted by becoming electronic themselves, while regulators addressed fragmentation, best execution, market data, and new forms of high-speed trading. The history of electronic trading shows that dissolving old physical boundaries can expand access without eliminating the need for coordination. As markets disperse, common standards for data, clearing, and investor protection become more important, not less. B Europe / United States / global banking ｜ 1988 onward

Historical event · story Basel capital and liquidity rules unfolded in Europe / United States / global banking during 1988 onward. International banks operate across national borders, but bank failures impose costs on domestic economies and depositors. By the 1980s, regulators worried that different national capital rules encouraged competitive weakening and made it difficult to compare bank resilience. The Basel Committee developed the 1988 Basel Accord, which set common risk-weighted capital standards for internationally active banks. Basel II added more risk sensitivity, and Basel III, developed after the 2008 crisis, increased capital quality and introduced leverage and liquidity standards. Capital and liquidity rules are financial limits intended to keep ordinary risk-taking from exhausting a bank’s capacity to absorb losses. The difficulty is setting constraints that are strong enough to improve resilience without freezing useful lending or pushing risk into less regulated sectors. Countries implemented the agreements through their own laws and regulations, so details differ. Banks raised capital, changed portfolios, and adapted funding structures, while critics debated complexity, risk weights, and unintended incentives. Basel standards continue to evolve because banking itself changes. Their history shows why limitations must be practical, transparent, and adjustable; overly weak rules fail in crisis, while excessively rigid rules can create new distortions. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. 61 中孚 | Hexagram 61

B United States ｜ 2001

Historical event · story Enron, auditing, and the crisis of trust unfolded in United States during 2001. Enron grew from a natural-gas company into a complex energy-trading and financial enterprise. Its reported earnings and share price rose rapidly, while executives used special-purpose entities and aggressive accounting that made the company’s true leverage and losses difficult for outsiders to see. In 2001 questions about related-party transactions and accounting intensified. Enron restated earnings, credit confidence collapsed, and the company filed for bankruptcy in December. Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, was convicted over document destruction, although the conviction was later overturned by the Supreme Court. The scandal was fundamentally about trust in reported numbers. Modern capital markets cannot independently inspect every underlying transaction, so investors rely on management, boards, auditors, and regulators to make financial statements credible. Employees and investors lost billions, and confidence in corporate reporting was badly damaged. Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002, strengthening audit oversight, executive certification, internal-control requirements, and penalties for misconduct. Enron’s collapse showed how quickly financing disappears when that credibility breaks. Rules can improve verification, but “inner truth” in finance ultimately depends on institutions that make deceptive reporting difficult and costly. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

62 小過 | Hexagram 62▶

62 小過 | Hexagram 62

B United States / global markets ｜ 1998

Historical event · story Long-Term Capital Management unfolded in United States / global markets during 1998. Long-Term Capital Management was a hedge fund founded in 1994 by experienced traders and prominent academics. It used sophisticated relative-value strategies that sought to profit from small price differences between related securities. Because expected price gaps were small, the fund used substantial leverage and derivatives to magnify returns. In 1998 the Russian financial crisis triggered large market moves and a flight to liquidity. Positions that were expected to converge instead moved further apart, producing severe losses. The striking feature was how “small” relative price differences became large balance-sheet risks when leverage was added. A strategy could be correct in long-run valuation terms yet fail if financing disappeared before prices converged. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York facilitated discussions among major creditors, and a private consortium recapitalized the fund. LTCM was wound down later. The episode did not require taxpayer capital, but it raised concern about counterparty exposure and hedge-fund leverage. LTCM became a standard case in risk management because it demonstrated that models, diversification, and famous expertise do not remove liquidity risk. Small expected gains can be overwhelmed by rare market moves when position size is too large. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

63 既濟 | Hexagram 63▶

63 既濟 | Hexagram 63

B European Union ｜ 1999–2002

Historical event · story Launch of the euro unfolded in European Union during 1999–2002. European integration had already created a large single market, but member states still used national currencies whose exchange-rate changes created transaction costs and periodic crises. The Maastricht Treaty set convergence criteria and a path toward monetary union. On 1 January 1999, eleven countries adopted the euro for electronic payments, accounting, and financial markets, while national notes and coins remained in circulation. Euro banknotes and coins entered public use in 2002, replacing participating national currencies. The launch was “after completion” only in a formal sense. Years of legal preparation, central-bank coordination, conversion of contracts, and technical work made the changeover possible, but the deeper economic integration required to support a common currency remained incomplete. The euro reduced exchange costs within the monetary union and created a large integrated capital market. It also removed national monetary and exchange-rate tools, so differences in productivity, fiscal policy, and banking conditions had to adjust through other channels. The sovereign-debt crisis later exposed weaknesses in banking and fiscal architecture, leading to new institutions and reforms. The euro’s history therefore shows that completing a major financial project often begins a new phase of maintenance and adaptation. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

64 未濟 | Hexagram 64▶

64 未濟 | Hexagram 64

B Euro area, Europe ｜ 2012 onward

Historical event · story European banking union after the sovereign-debt crisis unfolded in Euro area, Europe during 2012 onward. The euro-area sovereign-debt crisis revealed a damaging feedback loop between national governments and domestic banks. Weak banks could require public rescues, which strained government finances, while doubts about sovereign debt weakened the banks holding large amounts of it. European leaders agreed in 2012 to build a banking union. The European Central Bank assumed direct supervision of significant banks through the Single Supervisory Mechanism, and a Single Resolution Mechanism was created to manage failing banks with common procedures and a shared resolution fund. The project addressed an unfinished architecture: monetary union had centralized currency policy without fully centralizing bank supervision and crisis management. Banking union moved important responsibilities to the European level while leaving other protections partly national. The new system strengthened cross-border supervision and created tools for bank resolution, but the original banking-union agenda also included a common European deposit-insurance scheme that was not completed in the first phase. National differences in banking systems and fiscal risk remained politically sensitive. Its historical development is therefore a useful “before completion” case. Major pieces were built and used, yet the process showed that financial integration can proceed in stages, with each completed institution exposing the next unresolved boundary between national and shared responsibility. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

Western Cases

Line 1 — TW-EF-H01-L1 — XIANG-U-01-02▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H01-L1 — XIANG-U-01-02

001爻 Historical event Industrial Revolution in Britain unfolded in Britain, Europe during c. 1760–1840. Britain entered the eighteenth century with expanding Atlantic trade, agricultural change, coal resources, skilled craft traditions, and institutions capable of mobilizing private capital. Demand for textiles and other manufactured goods encouraged inventors and entrepreneurs to search for ways to raise output beyond the limits of hand production. Textile machinery, steam power, iron production, and factory organization developed over decades rather than in a single breakthrough. Investors financed mills, canals, mines, and machinery; workers moved toward industrial towns; and firms learned to coordinate larger quantities of labor, fuel, raw materials, and credit. The economic mechanism was cumulative: one improvement lowered costs or expanded capacity, which increased demand for transport, finance, and further machinery. Profits and retained earnings funded additional investment, while banks and partnerships helped bridge the gap between invention and commercial scale. Industrial production increased sharply and spread from Britain to continental Europe and North America. The change created new fortunes and new forms of wage labor, while also bringing crowded cities, dangerous working conditions, pollution, and repeated debates over labor law and social welfare. By the nineteenth century, industrialization had altered international trade and the relative economic weight of regions. Its gains were large but uneven, and later reforms addressed some of the social costs that early industrial growth had left unresolved. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

Line-specific comparison Line 1 begins with a compact image: the dragon lies hid in the deep; it is not the time for active doing: this appears from the strong and undivided lines being in the…. Set beside Industrial Revolution in Britain, the comparison shifts to productive capacity, investment, technology and the institutions that let innovation scale. The line therefore works best as a question of economic discipline: industrial transformation rewards capability only when capital, skills, infrastructure and markets can carry it. It does not tell investors, firms or governments what outcome is guaranteed, and it should not be treated as a trading signal or a claim that the historical actors consulted the Ten Wings. Instead, use the image to inspect the sequence of choices: what information was available, who carried the risk, which rule shaped behavior, and what consequences appeared after the first decision. What capability should remain unspent until the conditions for productive deployment are ready? This is a present-day editorial comparison. The historical source documents the economic event only; it does not document use of this line or the Ten Wings.

Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY. Source confirms the economic/financial event only. Historical reference ↗

004爻 Historical event Industrial Revolution in Britain unfolded in Britain, Europe during c. 1760–1840. Britain entered the eighteenth century with expanding Atlantic trade, agricultural change, coal resources, skilled craft traditions, and institutions capable of mobilizing private capital. Demand for textiles and other manufactured goods encouraged inventors and entrepreneurs to search for ways to raise output beyond the limits of hand production. Textile machinery, steam power, iron production, and factory organization developed over decades rather than in a single breakthrough. Investors financed mills, canals, mines, and machinery; workers moved toward industrial towns; and firms learned to coordinate larger quantities of labor, fuel, raw materials, and credit. The economic mechanism was cumulative: one improvement lowered costs or expanded capacity, which increased demand for transport, finance, and further machinery. Profits and retained earnings funded additional investment, while banks and partnerships helped bridge the gap between invention and commercial scale. Industrial production increased sharply and spread from Britain to continental Europe and North America. The change created new fortunes and new forms of wage labor, while also bringing crowded cities, dangerous working conditions, pollution, and repeated debates over labor law and social welfare. By the nineteenth century, industrialization had altered international trade and the relative economic weight of regions. Its gains were large but uneven, and later reforms addressed some of the social costs that early industrial growth had left unresolved. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

007爻 Historical event Solon's debt reforms at Athens unfolded in Athens, Europe during c. 594 BCE. Athens faced severe social conflict as small farmers fell into debt and some Athenians could be reduced to debt bondage. Concentrated landholding, creditor claims, and political exclusion made the existing order increasingly difficult to sustain. Solon was appointed archon and introduced measures traditionally associated with the seisachtheia, or “shaking off of burdens.” The reforms canceled certain debts secured on the person, prohibited debt slavery for Athenian citizens, and altered parts of the legal and political framework. The economic issue was not simply the size of debts but the way claims could convert financial distress into loss of personal freedom. By changing the enforceability and consequences of debt, the reforms redistributed bargaining power between creditors and debtors without eliminating private property or lending. The reforms did not create economic equality and did not end factional conflict. They did, however, change the rules surrounding personal debt and citizenship, and later Athenians remembered them as an important stage in the city’s constitutional development. Athens continued to experience political struggle after Solon, including the rise of Peisistratus. The longer-term significance of the reforms lay in establishing that debt rules were public institutions that could be revised when their social consequences threatened the wider civic order. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

013爻 Historical event Laurion silver and Athenian public finance unfolded in Attica, Europe during 5th century BCE. The silver mines at Laurion in Attica were a major source of revenue for Athens. In the early fifth century BCE, a rich new vein was discovered at a time when the city faced strategic choices over how to use unexpected income. Rather than distributing the entire windfall directly, Athenians accepted Themistocles’ proposal to direct substantial resources toward building a larger fleet. Mine revenues, leases, private contractors, slave labor, shipbuilding, and public decision-making became linked in a large mobilization of economic resources. This was a case of converting a volatile natural-resource windfall into durable productive and strategic assets. The decision required foregoing some immediate distribution in favor of ships, docks, skills, and an operating system that could be maintained over time. The fleet played a major role in the Persian Wars, especially at Salamis. Afterward, naval power supported Athenian influence and commerce, while the mining system continued to generate wealth under harsh labor conditions that modern readers must distinguish from the civic benefits enjoyed by citizens. The mines later declined and revived in different periods, and Athens’ wider empire eventually collapsed. The episode nevertheless remains a clear example of a polity debating whether a temporary revenue surge should be consumed immediately or invested in capacity with longer-lived effects. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

019爻 Historical event Roman grain supply and the annona unfolded in Rome, Europe during late Republic–Imperial era. As Rome grew, feeding a very large urban population became a recurring economic and political problem. Local production could not reliably supply the city, and harvest failures, transport disruption, speculation, or war could quickly raise the price of grain. Roman authorities gradually developed the annona: a complex system of procurement, shipping, storage, distribution, and later free or subsidized grain for eligible residents. Private merchants remained important, but the state organized incentives, contracts, port facilities, and administrative oversight to reduce the risk of shortages. Economically, the annona was neither a modern welfare state nor a fully state-run food system. It combined market exchange with public intervention, using purchasing power, legal privileges, storage, and distribution rules to manage a commodity whose shortage could threaten both household welfare and public order. The system helped sustain Rome’s population for centuries and tied the city to producing regions such as Sicily, North Africa, and Egypt. It also created heavy logistical obligations and made the capital dependent on long-distance supply lines and functioning ports. When political control and Mediterranean trade networks weakened in late antiquity, the scale and reliability of the system changed. Its long history shows how an essential good can require institutions that make ordinary commerce more resilient without eliminating private trade. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

Set beside Roman grain supply and the annona, the comparison shifts to food security, logistics, public provisioning and the administrative burden of supplying a large city. 025爻 Historical event The Medici Bank and patient network expansion unfolded in Florence and Europe during 1397–1494. Late medieval European commerce needed ways to move money across long distances despite dangerous travel, fragmented currencies, and church restrictions on explicit interest. Italian merchant-bankers developed bills of exchange, correspondent relationships, and branch networks to serve trade and elites. The Medici Bank expanded from Florence into important European centers. Its partners handled deposits, exchange, papal business, trade finance, and transfers between branches. Growth required detailed accounts, trusted managers, and careful balancing of local autonomy with central family oversight. Its operating model depended on waiting for information, settlement, and commercial opportunities to mature across distances. The institution could not treat every local request as equally attractive; liquidity and credit judgment had to be preserved while funds moved slowly through a network. For several decades the bank was among Europe’s most prominent financial institutions. Later, weak oversight and losses at some branches contributed to decline, and the bank was effectively dissolved by the end of the fifteenth century. The Medici experience became part of the broader history of European banking because it demonstrates both the power and fragility of branch finance before modern communications and regulation. Expansion created reach, but it also multiplied agency problems and delayed visibility into losses. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. The network later weakened as branches took on risks that the center could not always control and as political relationships changed. By the end of the fifteenth century the institution had declined. Its rise and fall showed both the advantages of an international banking network and the vulnerability created when distant managers, concentrated exposures and family politics outgrew oversight.

026爻 Historical event The Medici Bank and patient network expansion unfolded in Florence and Europe during 1397–1494. Late medieval European commerce needed ways to move money across long distances despite dangerous travel, fragmented currencies, and church restrictions on explicit interest. Italian merchant-bankers developed bills of exchange, correspondent relationships, and branch networks to serve trade and elites. The Medici Bank expanded from Florence into important European centers. Its partners handled deposits, exchange, papal business, trade finance, and transfers between branches. Growth required detailed accounts, trusted managers, and careful balancing of local autonomy with central family oversight. Its operating model depended on waiting for information, settlement, and commercial opportunities to mature across distances. The institution could not treat every local request as equally attractive; liquidity and credit judgment had to be preserved while funds moved slowly through a network. For several decades the bank was among Europe’s most prominent financial institutions. Later, weak oversight and losses at some branches contributed to decline, and the bank was effectively dissolved by the end of the fifteenth century. The Medici experience became part of the broader history of European banking because it demonstrates both the power and fragility of branch finance before modern communications and regulation. Expansion created reach, but it also multiplied agency problems and delayed visibility into losses. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. The network later weakened as branches took on risks that the center could not always control and as political relationships changed. By the end of the fifteenth century the institution had declined. Its rise and fall showed both the advantages of an international banking network and the vulnerability created when distant managers, concentrated exposures and family politics outgrew oversight.

031爻 Historical event Tulip speculation and contract disputes unfolded in Dutch Republic, Europe during 1636–1637. Tulips became fashionable luxury goods in the Dutch Republic, and rare varieties commanded high prices. By the mid-1630s, trading expanded from physical bulbs to agreements for future delivery, drawing in people beyond specialist growers. During the winter of 1636–1637, prices for some contracts rose quickly. Trading often took place in informal settings, and participants could enter agreements without immediate delivery. In February 1637, demand weakened abruptly at auctions, and prices fell as buyers resisted completing contracts at earlier prices. The central economic problem was contractual conflict after expectations changed. A rising market had made obligations appear easy to honor; falling prices exposed the difference between a quoted contract value and the ability or willingness of counterparties to settle. The collapse produced disputes over enforcement and settlement. Authorities and market participants sought compromises, and many contracts were not enforced at their original terms. The episode damaged some participants but did not destroy the Dutch economy, contrary to later popular myths. Later retellings exaggerated the scale of the event, but the surviving record still illustrates how speculative markets can generate legal uncertainty when trading conventions develop faster than clear rules for margin, settlement, and default. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line-specific comparison Line 1 begins with a compact image: The line does not perpetuate the matter about which the contention is: contention should not be prolonged.. 043爻 Historical event Bretton Woods monetary cooperation unfolded in United States / Europe during 1944. The interwar period had shown how competitive devaluations, exchange controls, war debts, and collapsing trade could deepen international instability. As the Second World War continued, Allied governments began planning a monetary order intended to support reconstruction and reduce destructive currency conflict. Delegates from forty-four countries met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944. They negotiated a system of fixed but adjustable exchange rates centered on the U.S. dollar, and created the International Monetary Fund and the institution that became the World Bank. The arrangement worked because states accepted shared rules and institutions rather than relying only on bilateral deals. Cooperation reduced uncertainty for trade and investment, while the IMF offered a mechanism for temporary balance-of-payments support. The system began operating after the war. It helped provide a framework for exchange-rate stability and reconstruction, though countries retained controls and adjusted parities when necessary. By the late 1960s, strains grew as global dollar claims exceeded confidence in U.S. gold convertibility. In 1971 the United States suspended dollar convertibility into gold, and the fixed-rate system gave way to more flexible exchange rates. The Bretton Woods institutions survived, showing that a cooperative framework can outlast the specific monetary rule that originally brought members together. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

Set beside Bretton Woods monetary cooperation, the comparison shifts to international monetary coordination, exchange-rate rules, liquidity support and the governance of shared institutions. The historical case shows decisions unfolding through institutions, prices, contracts, capital and practical constraints rather than through a single dramatic moment. The line therefore works best as a question of economic discipline: cooperation can stabilize trade, but only if members accept common rules and mechanisms for adjustment. 048爻 Historical event Bretton Woods monetary cooperation unfolded in United States / Europe during 1944. The interwar period had shown how competitive devaluations, exchange controls, war debts, and collapsing trade could deepen international instability. As the Second World War continued, Allied governments began planning a monetary order intended to support reconstruction and reduce destructive currency conflict. Delegates from forty-four countries met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944. They negotiated a system of fixed but adjustable exchange rates centered on the U.S. dollar, and created the International Monetary Fund and the institution that became the World Bank. The arrangement worked because states accepted shared rules and institutions rather than relying only on bilateral deals. Cooperation reduced uncertainty for trade and investment, while the IMF offered a mechanism for temporary balance-of-payments support. The system began operating after the war. It helped provide a framework for exchange-rate stability and reconstruction, though countries retained controls and adjusted parities when necessary. By the late 1960s, strains grew as global dollar claims exceeded confidence in U.S. gold convertibility. In 1971 the United States suspended dollar convertibility into gold, and the fixed-rate system gave way to more flexible exchange rates. The Bretton Woods institutions survived, showing that a cooperative framework can outlast the specific monetary rule that originally brought members together. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. 049爻 Historical event Early savings banks in Britain and Europe unfolded in Britain / Europe during late 18th–early 19th century. Industrialization and urbanization created a growing population of wage earners who needed safe places to hold small amounts of money. Traditional private banks often served merchants and wealthy clients rather than workers with modest, irregular savings. Philanthropic and mutual savings institutions began to appear in Britain and parts of Europe. They accepted small deposits, kept individual accounts, and invested pooled funds in relatively conservative assets. Rules often limited withdrawals or the size of balances to preserve the institutions’ intended social purpose. The model showed how many small contributions could accumulate into a meaningful pool of capital. It depended less on one spectacular investment than on regular deposits, record keeping, trust, and conservative management. Savings banks spread during the nineteenth century and later became more formal parts of national financial systems. Their exact structures differed by country, and many eventually merged, commercialized, or came under stronger regulation. For households, the innovation made saving more practical and visible. For the wider economy, pooled deposits could be invested rather than kept idle. The institutions also foreshadowed later debates about deposit safety, access to finance, and the boundary between social purpose and commercial banking. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

055爻 Historical event The South Sea Bubble unfolded in Britain, Europe during 1720. Britain emerged from long wars with a large public debt. The South Sea Company proposed to assume portions of that debt in exchange for government privileges and the opportunity to convert creditors into company shareholders. Expectations about trade and financial engineering helped lift the share price. In 1720 the company carried out large debt-conversion schemes while its shares rose dramatically. Credit, installment purchases, promotional claims, and a wider boom in new companies encouraged speculation. Parliament also passed the Bubble Act, partly in a climate shaped by competition for investor money. The episode turned an apparently technical debt-management plan into a highly leveraged speculative market. Each rise in the share price made further conversion look easier, but the structure became vulnerable once expectations stopped supporting the valuation. The South Sea share price collapsed later that year. Investors suffered heavy losses, politicians and company officials faced investigation, and Parliament restructured the company. The British state did not default, and parts of the public debt were reorganized under other institutions. The aftermath produced inquiries and reforms rather than the end of British finance. The event became a lasting example of how complex balance-sheet transactions can appear routine during a boom yet carry large consequences when market confidence changes. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

061爻 Historical event Postwar European economic expansion unfolded in Western Europe during c. 1950–1973. Europe emerged from the Second World War with damaged infrastructure, displaced populations, shortages, and heavy public debts. Reconstruction required capital, imported food and machinery, functioning currencies, and political arrangements that could support trade rather than renewed economic fragmentation. National reconstruction programs, Marshall Plan assistance, currency reforms, investment, expanding education, and strong demand contributed to rapid growth. European countries also reduced trade barriers through new institutions, while firms adopted technologies and production methods that had advanced during and after the war. The expansion depended on several forces arriving together: restored demand, investment, stable institutions, demographic change, and access to international markets. No single policy produced the entire boom, and outcomes varied across countries. For roughly two decades, much of Western Europe experienced high productivity growth, rising real wages, expanding welfare systems, and increasing household consumption. Growth rates eventually slowed in the 1970s as the postwar catch-up phase matured and oil shocks intensified inflation. The period left Europe with higher living standards, deeper regional integration, and larger public commitments. It also created expectations of continued growth that became harder to meet when inflation and slower productivity arrived in the following decade. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

067爻 Historical event The Great Depression unfolded in United States / Europe during 1929–1930s. The late 1920s combined rapid industrial growth, rising equity prices, heavy use of credit in some markets, agricultural weakness, and an international monetary system constrained by the gold standard. Financial vulnerabilities differed by country, but the global economy was already fragile when U.S. share prices fell in 1929. The stock-market crash was followed by banking failures, collapsing investment, falling prices, and severe unemployment. As banks failed, deposits and credit disappeared. International trade contracted sharply, and policy responses such as tariff increases and adherence to gold in several countries limited adjustment. The crisis was not one event but a chain in which financial contraction, falling demand, debt burdens, and policy constraints reinforced one another. A system that had appeared prosperous lost the flows of credit and spending that had kept businesses and households connected. The downturn became the deepest economic contraction of the modern industrial era. Countries left the gold standard at different times, governments adopted new banking and relief measures, and recovery proceeded unevenly. Full employment in many countries arrived only with wartime mobilization. The Depression transformed economic policy and financial regulation across the United States and Europe. It also left a durable political memory: when money, credit, employment, and trade all contract together, restoring coordination becomes harder than repairing any one market in isolation. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

It does not tell investors, firms or governments what outcome is guaranteed, and it should not be treated as a trading signal or a claim that the historical actors consulted the Ten Wings. 073爻 Historical event The Buttonwood Agreement and early U.S. securities trading unfolded in New York, United States during 1792. After the American Revolution, federal and state securities, bank shares, and other financial claims began trading in New York. The young market lacked a centralized exchange, and brokers competed for commissions and access to buyers and sellers. In May 1792, twenty-four brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement. They promised to give preference to one another in securities transactions and set a minimum commission. The arrangement was small, but it formalized a network of intermediaries who regularly met and dealt with one another. The economic value came from creating a more predictable community of counterparties. Repeated dealing reduced some search costs and helped concentrate information and liquidity, though it also created a club whose access and rules were controlled by members. The group evolved through later organizations into what became the New York Stock Exchange. Trading rules, membership standards, listing practices, and technology changed enormously over time, but the early agreement became part of the institutional history of organized U.S. securities markets. As U.S. capital markets grew, organized exchanges became important channels for corporate finance and investment. The Buttonwood story is modest in scale, yet it shows how markets often begin with people agreeing on procedures before they build elaborate institutions. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

079爻 Historical event The California Gold Rush unfolded in California, United States during 1848–1855. Gold was discovered at Sutter’s Mill in January 1848, just as California passed from Mexican to U.S. control. News spread rapidly, and the prospect of extracting valuable metal attracted migrants from across the United States, Latin America, Europe, China, and elsewhere. Hundreds of thousands of people arrived. Some mined directly; many others supplied food, tools, transport, lodging, banking, and other services. San Francisco expanded quickly, prices for scarce goods rose, and capital moved into mining techniques that required more equipment than individual prospectors could provide. Gold functioned both as a commodity and as monetary wealth. The rush drew labor and capital toward a region where property rights, infrastructure, and public institutions were still being established, producing both extraordinary opportunity and high uncertainty. Early surface deposits became harder to find, and larger firms increasingly used capital-intensive methods. The rush accelerated California’s population growth and statehood, enriched some participants, ruined others, and caused severe displacement and violence against Indigenous communities. The long-term effects included new cities, transport links, businesses, and integration with national and Pacific trade. The event also demonstrated that a sudden abundance of valuable resources does not distribute itself evenly; complementary skills, infrastructure, timing, and legal control shape who captures the gains. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

085爻 Historical event John Bogle and the first retail index mutual fund unfolded in United States during 1976. By the 1970s, academic research had raised doubts about whether most professional managers could reliably beat broad market indexes after fees. Mutual funds were already widely used, but active management and sales charges remained common for individual investors. John C. Bogle, leading the newly formed Vanguard Group, launched First Index Investment Trust in 1976. The fund sought to track the S&P 500 rather than select stocks. Its initial offering attracted far less money than the organizers had hoped, and critics mocked the idea as settling for average performance. The innovation was deliberately modest: own a broad market, reduce turnover, and keep costs low. Its promise did not depend on identifying the next winning company; it depended on minimizing the gap between the market return and the investor’s net return. The fund survived, later became Vanguard 500 Index Fund, and was followed by many other index products. Over subsequent decades, low-cost passive investing grew into a major part of U.S. and global asset management. Index funds did not eliminate active investing, market cycles, or investor mistakes. They did, however, change the competitive benchmark for the fund industry by making fees, diversification, and tracking accuracy more visible to ordinary investors. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

091爻 Historical event The dot-com boom unfolded in United States / Europe during 1995–2000. The commercialization of the internet created genuine new businesses and a plausible belief that communications, retail, media, and finance would be transformed. Falling technology costs and strong venture-capital markets made it easier for young firms to raise money before they had long operating histories. Investors bid up shares of technology and internet companies. Initial public offerings multiplied, media attention intensified, and companies emphasized user growth, market share, or future network effects even when current profits were limited. European technology markets joined the enthusiasm, though the largest valuations centered in the United States. The boom mixed authentic technological progress with financial extrapolation. Capital was abundant enough to fund experimentation, but high valuations reduced the margin for disappointment. When expected growth failed to arrive quickly enough, financing conditions changed before the underlying technology disappeared. The NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 and then fell sharply. Many companies failed, venture funding contracted, and investors lost large sums. At the same time, surviving firms and the infrastructure built during the boom continued to support later internet growth. The aftermath separated the internet as a durable technology from the prices investors had been willing to pay for many early companies. The episode became a reminder that enthusiasm can accelerate innovation while also weakening valuation discipline. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. 092爻 Historical event The dot-com boom unfolded in United States / Europe during 1995–2000. The commercialization of the internet created genuine new businesses and a plausible belief that communications, retail, media, and finance would be transformed. Line 1 — TW-EF-H17-L1 — XIANG-U-17-02

097爻 Historical event The rise of index investing unfolded in United States / Europe during 1970s onward. Institutional investors and academics increasingly measured portfolio performance against broad indexes during the 1960s and 1970s. Evidence that many active portfolios underperformed after costs encouraged experiments with strategies that simply replicated a market benchmark. Early indexed institutional portfolios were followed by retail mutual funds and, later, exchange-traded funds. As computing improved and trading costs fell, providers could track increasingly specialized indexes while charging lower fees than many traditional active funds. The core mechanism is following a predefined rule rather than making repeated forecasts about individual securities. That changes where judgment is exercised: from daily stock selection toward choice of index, asset allocation, rebalancing, taxes, and investor behavior. Passive investing expanded dramatically in the United States and Europe. It reduced costs for many investors and made diversification easier, while also creating new debates about index construction, corporate voting power, concentration, and the effects of large automatic flows. Indexing did not make markets passive in a literal sense; prices still depend on active trading and new information. Its historical importance lies in making “follow the market at low cost” a mainstream alternative to paying managers to attempt to beat it. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

The line therefore works best as a question of economic discipline: following a broad market can be rational when the rule is explicit, low-cost and consistent with the investor's objective. It does not tell investors, firms or governments what outcome is guaranteed, and it should not be treated as a trading signal or a claim that the historical actors consulted the Ten Wings. Instead, use the image to inspect the sequence of choices: what information was available, who carried the risk, which rule shaped behavior, and what consequences appeared after the first decision. Continuation edition · 7 October 2026 · 100 records

This continuation covers Small Image (Xiao Xiang) line records 101–200 in King Wen order: Lines 5–6 of Hexagram 17, all six lines of Hexagrams 18–33, and Lines 1–2 of Hexagram 34. It preserves the original Chinese Small Image text, the supplied English translation, and the source-unit numbering used in the earlier 384-line political and military edition.

Each hexagram is paired with one economic, financial, business, market, banking, public-finance, monetary, or investment case from Europe or the United States. The same historical case is shared across the six lines of its hexagram where applicable, while every Line-specific comparison is separately written for that Small Image.

Every Historical event is a 300–500-word very short historical story. The narrative is checked for cause/background, course of events, and aftermath; it does not invent dialogue, private thoughts, or dramatic scenes. Every Line-specific comparison is a 150–200-word social-post-style retrospective analogy. Historical references establish event facts only, not historical use of the Ten Wings.

Evidence status is RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY for every record. The economic and financial comparisons are contemporary editorial readings and should not be presented as investment advice, historical causation by the Zhouyi, or proof that the participants consulted the text.

RWD rule: ≥768 px show Original Chinese and English translation side by side. <768 px stack in reading order: Original Chinese → English translation → Historical event → Line-specific comparison → Historical reference. Use at least 16 px body text on phones, line-height ≥1.5, no horizontal scrolling, and narrative panels that grow with content.

Recommended route: /en/ten-wings/line-images/economics-finance/{hexagram_no}/{line_no}. Keep immutable IDs, semantic headings, lang="zh-Hant" for Chinese and lang="en" for English, keyboard-focusable source links, and an exposed evidence badge. Word page breaks are editorial only and have no meaning in the app.

103爻 Historical event Glass-Steagall banking reform unfolded in United States during 1933. After thousands of U.S. banks failed during the Great Depression, public confidence in the banking system was severely damaged. Investigations also focused attention on conflicts involving securities underwriting, bank affiliates, and speculative activity during the 1920s. The Banking Act of 1933 created federal deposit insurance and included provisions commonly called Glass-Steagall that separated important commercial-banking and investment-banking activities. The law changed institutional structures while emergency programs and bank examinations worked to stabilize surviving banks. The reform addressed a damaged system by changing underlying rules rather than simply restarting old practices. Deposit insurance targeted runs, while structural restrictions sought to reduce conflicts and limit certain combinations of risk inside deposit-taking organizations. Bank failures fell sharply as the financial system recovered, though many factors contributed. Over the following decades, market innovation and regulatory changes blurred some boundaries. Key Glass-Steagall affiliation restrictions were repealed by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act in 1999. Debate over the law’s later repeal continues, especially in discussions of the 2008 crisis. Whatever interpretation one takes, the 1933 legislation is a clear example of policymakers responding to institutional decay with redesigned safeguards rather than a temporary patch alone. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. 109爻 Historical event The Marshall Plan unfolded in United States / Western Europe during 1948–1952. After the Second World War, European economies faced damaged infrastructure, shortages, weak trade, and shortages of dollars needed to buy food, fuel, and machinery. Political instability and a severe winter added urgency to the reconstruction problem. The United States created the European Recovery Program, commonly known as the Marshall Plan. Participating countries received aid and worked through European institutions to coordinate needs and recovery programs. Funds supported imports, investment, technical assistance, and efforts to restore production and trade. The program brought outside resources close to economies that still had local skills, firms, labor, and administrative capacity. Aid mattered because it could be combined with domestic reforms and rebuilding rather than replacing them. European recovery was already beginning in some places, and historians do not attribute the entire postwar boom to American aid. The program nevertheless eased critical constraints, supported investment, and encouraged forms of economic cooperation that later deepened. By the early 1950s, industrial production had risen substantially and the emergency phase of reconstruction was ending. The Marshall Plan also strengthened transatlantic economic ties and became a reference point in later debates about when external assistance can catalyze recovery. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

112爻 Historical event The Marshall Plan unfolded in United States / Western Europe during 1948–1952. After the Second World War, European economies faced damaged infrastructure, shortages, weak trade, and shortages of dollars needed to buy food, fuel, and machinery. Political instability and a severe winter added urgency to the reconstruction problem. The United States created the European Recovery Program, commonly known as the Marshall Plan. Participating countries received aid and worked through European institutions to coordinate needs and recovery programs. Funds supported imports, investment, technical assistance, and efforts to restore production and trade. The program brought outside resources close to economies that still had local skills, firms, labor, and administrative capacity. By the early 1950s, industrial production had risen substantially and the emergency phase of reconstruction was ending. The Marshall Plan also strengthened transatlantic economic ties and became a reference point in later debates about when external assistance can catalyze recovery.
