115爻 Historical event SEC disclosure after the 1929 crash unfolded in United States during 1933–1934. The 1929 crash and subsequent investigations exposed abusive market practices, weak disclosure, and conflicts in securities distribution. Many investors had purchased securities with limited standardized information about issuers or the interests of intermediaries. Congress passed the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The second law created the Securities and Exchange Commission. The new framework required registration and periodic disclosure for many public securities and regulated exchanges, brokers, and market practices. The economic premise was that investors need a common information baseline to evaluate securities. Public filing rules made financial statements and material facts more observable, while enforcement created consequences for manipulation and misrepresentation. The federal securities regime did not guarantee investment success or prevent market declines. Instead, it established disclosure, anti-fraud, and market-oversight rules that became central to U.S. capital markets and later evolved as products and technology changed. Over time, disclosure expanded to electronic filing, governance requirements, insider rules, and specialized reporting. The basic institutional idea remained: market participants can make their own judgments, but the market functions better when material information is not left entirely to private rumor and salesmanship. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. 121爻 Historical event Standard Oil antitrust breakup unfolded in United States during 1911. By the late nineteenth century, Standard Oil had become the dominant U.S. oil-refining organization through acquisitions, contracts, logistics advantages, and aggressive competitive practices. Critics argued that its scale and conduct restrained competition. The federal government sued under the Sherman Antitrust Act. In 1911 the U.S. Supreme Court held that Standard Oil had violated the law and ordered the combination dissolved into separate companies. The decision applied a “rule of reason” approach to restraints of trade. The economic issue was how to distinguish efficiency gained from scale from market power maintained through exclusionary conduct. The remedy did not abolish oil refining; it changed corporate boundaries and the competitive structure in which assets operated. The successor companies continued to operate, and several later became major oil corporations in their own right. The breakup did not end concentration debates, but it demonstrated that federal antitrust law could be used against a powerful integrated enterprise. Antitrust policy continued to evolve through later statutes and cases. Standard Oil became a foundational story in U.S. competition policy because it showed law “biting through” a complex corporate structure rather than merely criticizing concentrated power. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. 127爻 Historical event Coca-Cola public listing and brand finance unfolded in United States during 1919. By the early twentieth century, Coca-Cola had developed from a fountain drink into a nationally recognized branded product supported by bottling networks and advertising. Expansion required capital for production, distribution, and the organization of a growing corporate system. In 1919 a group of investors acquired the company, and shares of The Coca-Cola Company were offered publicly. Over time the firm used branding, standardized products, bottler relationships, and extensive marketing to build consumer recognition across the United States and eventually overseas. The economic mechanism joined a physical product to an intangible asset: the brand. Advertising and distribution could increase the value of each other because consumer recognition made shelf space and bottling more productive, while wider availability reinforced the brand. The company survived major shifts in tastes, regulation, war, and competition and became one of the most recognized consumer brands in the world. Its share history also became associated with long-term compounding, dividends, and the value investors place on durable intangible assets. The case also shows the limits of appearance alone. Brand value must be supported by product consistency, distribution, pricing, and financial discipline. A polished image can attract attention, but only operating results can sustain the economic value attached to that image. 139爻 Historical event U.S. recovery after the Panic of 1907 unfolded in United States during 1907–1908. A weakening economy and failed speculative efforts involving United Copper undermined confidence in several New York financial institutions. Trust companies, which had grown rapidly but held smaller cash reserves than national banks, became particularly vulnerable to runs. Depositors withdrew funds and credit markets froze. Financier J. P. Morgan coordinated private pools of liquidity with banks, trust companies, and the U.S. Treasury to support key institutions and the New York Stock Exchange. Some firms failed, but broader collapse was avoided. The immediate recovery depended on restoring circulation of cash and credit. Private coordination could temporarily reconnect institutions, but the effort relied heavily on a few individuals and could not guarantee a repeatable response to future national crises. The panic subsided, yet the episode convinced many policymakers that the United States needed a more systematic lender-of-last-resort structure. The National Monetary Commission studied reform, and Congress eventually created the Federal Reserve System in 1913. What returned after the panic was not simply market confidence; it was a policy agenda. The financial system resumed normal operations, while the memory of how close it had come to paralysis helped generate institutional change. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

143爻 Historical event U.S. recovery after the Panic of 1907 unfolded in United States during 1907–1908. A weakening economy and failed speculative efforts involving United Copper undermined confidence in several New York financial institutions. Trust companies, which had grown rapidly but held smaller cash reserves than national banks, became particularly vulnerable to runs. Depositors withdrew funds and credit markets froze. Financier J. P. Morgan coordinated private pools of liquidity with banks, trust companies, and the U.S. Treasury to support key institutions and the New York Stock Exchange. Some firms failed, but broader collapse was avoided. The immediate recovery depended on restoring circulation of cash and credit. The panic subsided, yet the episode convinced many policymakers that the United States needed a more systematic lender-of-last-resort structure. The National Monetary Commission studied reform, and Congress eventually created the Federal Reserve System in 1913. What returned after the panic was not simply market confidence; it was a policy agenda. The financial system resumed normal operations, while the memory of how close it had come to paralysis helped generate institutional change. 145爻 Historical event Black Monday unfolded in United States / Europe during 19 October 1987. Equity markets had risen strongly during the mid-1980s, while concerns were growing about valuation, interest rates, trade imbalances, and market structure. New portfolio-insurance strategies and computerized trading linked selling decisions more tightly to market declines. On 19 October 1987 the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6 percent in one day, and major markets in Europe and elsewhere also suffered extraordinary losses. Order imbalances, delayed price information, futures-market interactions, and automated selling amplified uncertainty. The shock was “unexpected” in timing and scale even though risks had been visible. Once prices moved sharply, strategies designed to reduce individual portfolio risk could collectively add to market selling, demonstrating how protective rules can interact in ways no participant intends. The Federal Reserve publicly stated its readiness to provide liquidity, and markets stabilized without a depression or wave of major bank failures. Regulators later studied market links, clearing capacity, and trading mechanisms, contributing to the development of coordinated circuit breakers. The 1987 crash became an important test of modern market plumbing. It did not end equity investing, but it changed how exchanges and regulators prepared for rapid price moves and how investors thought about liquidity during extreme stress. 151爻 Historical event Creation of the Federal Reserve System unfolded in United States during 1913. The United States suffered repeated banking panics in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Its fragmented banking structure, seasonal demand for currency, and absence of a permanent central liquidity mechanism made credit conditions unstable during periods of fear. After the Panic of 1907, reform studies intensified. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 created a system of regional Federal Reserve Banks overseen by a federal board. The design reflected political compromise between demands for centralized authority and distrust of concentrated financial power. Creating the Fed was an act of institutional accumulation: reserves, information, payment functions, and authority were organized so they could be deployed across the banking system rather than remaining scattered among private banks. The new system began operations in 1914. Its responsibilities changed substantially over time, especially after the Great Depression and later legislation, but the Federal Reserve became the central institution for U.S. monetary policy, bank reserves, and emergency liquidity. The institution did not prevent future crises, and its policies have often been debated. Its historical importance lies in replacing ad hoc crisis coordination with a durable public framework capable of storing financial capacity for moments when private liquidity disappears. Its fragmented banking structure, seasonal demand for currency, and absence of a permanent central liquidity mechanism made credit conditions unstable during periods of fear. After the Panic of 1907, reform studies intensified. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 created a system of regional Federal Reserve Banks overseen by a federal board. The design reflected political compromise between demands for centralized authority and distrust of concentrated financial power. Creating the Fed was an act of institutional accumulation: reserves, information, payment functions, and authority were organized so they could be deployed across the banking system rather than remaining scattered among private banks. The new system began operations in 1914. Its responsibilities changed substantially over time, especially after the Great Depression and later legislation, but the Federal Reserve became the central institution for U.S. monetary policy, bank reserves, and emergency liquidity. The institution did not prevent future crises, and its policies have often been debated. Its historical importance lies in replacing ad hoc crisis coordination with a durable public framework capable of storing financial capacity for moments when private liquidity disappears. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

157爻 Historical event Roman grain distribution to the urban population unfolded in Rome, Europe during 1st century BCE–3rd century CE. Rome’s population depended on regular supplies of grain, oil, and other staples arriving from across the Mediterranean. Poor harvests or interrupted shipping could quickly become both a household crisis and a political problem in the capital. The Roman state developed eligibility lists, distribution points, port and warehouse infrastructure, shipping incentives, and administrative offices to keep food moving. The system changed across centuries and rulers, but the underlying objective was to maintain a dependable flow of basic nourishment into the city. Economically, nourishment depended on logistics as much as production. Grain had to be grown, purchased or collected, transported, protected from spoilage, stored, and distributed to the intended recipients at a predictable time. The annona supported urban life on a scale that local agriculture alone could not sustain. It also required taxes, procurement, shipping, storage, and control over key producing regions, making food security part of imperial administration. Later political fragmentation reduced the scale of these systems in the western empire. The long record shows that “feeding” an economy is a chain: if finance, transport, storage, or administration fails, the existence of food somewhere else does not solve the immediate problem. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line 1 — TW-EF-H28-L1 — XIANG-U-28-02 — Record 163▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H28-L1 — XIANG-U-28-02 — Record 163

163爻 Historical event The 2008 global leverage crisis unfolded in United States / Europe during 2007–2009. Before 2007, low interest rates, strong demand for mortgage securities, rising house prices, and financial engineering encouraged a large expansion of housing credit. Banks and nonbank institutions used leverage and short-term funding to hold securities whose risks were difficult to assess once housing prices stopped rising. Mortgage delinquencies increased, structured products lost value, and institutions became reluctant to lend to one another. Bear Stearns failed and was sold in March 2008; Lehman Brothers failed in September; AIG required government support; and banks in Europe also came under severe pressure. The system had become “too heavy” because large positions rested on thin capital cushions and confidence in continuous refinancing. When asset values fell, institutions had to shrink balance sheets precisely when many others were trying to do the same. Governments guaranteed liabilities, recapitalized banks, created asset-purchase and liquidity programs, and used fiscal stimulus. The recession was deep, unemployment rose, and public debt increased. Recovery took years and differed across countries. Post-crisis reforms raised capital and liquidity requirements and added resolution planning and stress testing. 169爻 Historical event Bank failures during the Great Depression unfolded in United States during 1930–1933. As the U.S. economy contracted after 1929, loan losses rose and public confidence weakened. Deposits were not federally insured, and many small banks were exposed to local economic conditions or held assets that could not easily be sold without losses. Waves of deposit withdrawals forced banks to seek cash. Institutions that could not meet withdrawals suspended operations or failed, destroying deposits and reducing credit. By early 1933 the crisis was so severe that states declared banking holidays, followed by a national bank holiday after Franklin Roosevelt took office. A bank run turns fear into a mechanical liquidity problem. Even assets that may pay over time cannot always be converted to cash fast enough to satisfy simultaneous withdrawals, and forced sales can create additional losses. Congress passed emergency banking legislation, solvent banks reopened after review, and federal deposit insurance was established later in 1933. Confidence improved, but the earlier failures had already intensified the Depression by contracting money and credit. The episode became a core lesson in modern banking policy: danger is not only bad loans but also the mismatch between long-lived assets and deposits redeemable on demand. Deposit insurance and lender-of-last-resort facilities were later designed partly to prevent that abyss from reopening. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

174爻 Historical event Bank failures during the Great Depression unfolded in United States during 1930–1933. As the U.S. economy contracted after 1929, loan losses rose and public confidence weakened. Deposits were not federally insured, and many small banks were exposed to local economic conditions or held assets that could not easily be sold without losses. Waves of deposit withdrawals forced banks to seek cash. Institutions that could not meet withdrawals suspended operations or failed, destroying deposits and reducing credit. By early 1933 the crisis was so severe that states declared banking holidays, followed by a national bank holiday after Franklin Roosevelt took office. A bank run turns fear into a mechanical liquidity problem. Even assets that may pay over time cannot always be converted to cash fast enough to satisfy simultaneous withdrawals, and forced sales can create additional losses. Congress passed emergency banking legislation, solvent banks reopened after review, and federal deposit insurance was established later in 1933. Confidence improved, but the earlier failures had already intensified the Depression by contracting money and credit. The episode became a core lesson in modern banking policy: danger is not only bad loans but also the mismatch between long-lived assets and deposits redeemable on demand. Deposit insurance and lender-of-last-resort facilities were later designed partly to prevent that abyss from reopening. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

175爻 Historical event The international gold standard unfolded in United States / Europe during 1870s–1930s. By the late nineteenth century, many major economies linked their currencies to fixed quantities of gold. The system supported predictable exchange rates and facilitated international trade and investment during an era of expanding global capital flows. Central banks and treasuries maintained convertibility by holding gold reserves and adjusting interest rates or domestic credit when gold moved across borders. The system worked differently in each country and relied on confidence that authorities would defend the stated parity. Gold provided an external monetary anchor, but it also bound domestic policy to reserve flows. When confidence was strong, the rule could support stable exchange rates; when economies contracted, the same rule could transmit deflation and restrict policy choices. The First World War disrupted convertibility. Attempts to restore the prewar system in the 1920s proved fragile, and during the Great Depression the obligation to defend gold often conflicted with the need to support banks, prices, and employment. Britain left gold in 1931; the United States changed policy in 1933. The classical system did not return after the Depression. Its history remains important because it shows the trade-off between “clinging” to a fixed monetary anchor and preserving flexibility when domestic financial conditions change sharply. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

181爻 Historical event The Rothschild banking network unfolded in Britain / France / Europe during late 18th–19th century. European states, merchants, and investors needed reliable ways to transfer funds across borders during an era of slow communication, multiple currencies, and frequent war. Family and correspondent networks could reduce the risks of dealing with distant counterparties. Mayer Amschel Rothschild’s sons established banking houses in major European cities, including London, Paris, Vienna, Naples, and Frankfurt. The houses exchanged information, moved bullion and bills, placed government loans, and coordinated transactions through close family ties and trusted agents. The economic advantage came from influence built on information, reputation, and repeated settlement. A credible network could persuade distant parties to accept claims because members expected the wider family system to honor obligations and transmit funds. The network became highly influential in nineteenth-century sovereign finance and infrastructure funding. Its prominence later changed as joint-stock banks, public markets, and new financial institutions expanded. The story is often surrounded by myth and conspiracy claims that should be rejected. The Bank evolved through repeated changes in law and practice. It handled government finance, issued notes, interacted with commercial banks, and gradually developed central-banking functions. The Bank Charter Act of 1844 reshaped note issuance, while later crises expanded expectations that it would support market liquidity. Its durability came not from remaining unchanged but from preserving institutional continuity while functions adapted. Credibility accumulated through centuries of payments, government finance, reserve management, and crisis response. The institution survived wars, financial panics, the end of gold convertibility, nationalization in 1946, and operational independence for monetary policy in 1997. Its role today is very different from its original charter. The Bank of England illustrates a particular kind of financial constancy: rules and tools can change while an institution keeps serving a recognizable public function. Long duration therefore depends on adaptation within a stable legal and reputational framework. Line 1 — TW-EF-H33-L1 — XIANG-U-33-02 — Record 193

193爻 Historical event Britain leaves the gold standard unfolded in Britain, Europe during 1931. Britain returned to the gold standard in 1925 at the prewar parity, but the economy struggled with weak competitiveness, unemployment, and pressure on the balance of payments. The global Depression after 1929 intensified these strains. In 1931, financial pressure and loss of confidence led to heavy gold outflows. The government and Bank of England raised rates and sought foreign credits, but reserves continued to fall. In September, Britain suspended gold convertibility and allowed sterling to depreciate. Economically, retreat from gold meant abandoning a prestigious rule to preserve room for adjustment. It imposed losses and uncertainty on some holders of sterling but reduced the need to defend an exchange rate through deeper domestic deflation. The departure ended the obligation to exchange sterling for gold at the old parity. Sterling’s fall improved some competitive conditions, and monetary policy gained more room to support the domestic economy. Other countries later left gold as the Depression continued. The episode became a major turning point in the breakup of the interwar gold standard. It shows that withdrawal can be a policy decision rather than simple defeat when maintaining the existing commitment threatens the wider system. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

199爻 Historical event The dollar-centered Bretton Woods order unfolded in United States / Europe during 1944–1971. The Second World War left the United States with a large share of global gold reserves and industrial capacity. Policymakers designing the postwar monetary system wanted stable exchange rates without recreating the rigidities and competitive devaluations of the interwar period. Under Bretton Woods, participating currencies were fixed to the U.S. dollar within agreed bands, while the dollar was convertible into gold for foreign monetary authorities at $35 per ounce. The arrangement placed the dollar at the center of global reserves and settlement. The system gave the United States extraordinary monetary power, but that strength came with a constraint: the issuer of the reserve currency had to supply dollars to the world while also supporting belief that those dollars could be converted into gold. As Europe and Japan recovered, global trade and dollar holdings expanded. By the 1960s, foreign dollar claims grew relative to U.S. gold reserves, creating tension between providing world liquidity and maintaining confidence in convertibility. In August 1971 President Richard Nixon suspended gold convertibility. The fixed-rate system ended soon afterward, but the dollar remained the dominant reserve and transaction currency. Great monetary power therefore outlasted the particular rule that once defined it. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

The state financed construction largely through bonds and dedicated revenues. Engineers built hundreds of miles of canal, locks, and aqueducts across difficult terrain. When the canal opened in 1825, shipping costs and travel times between the Great Lakes region and the Atlantic fell sharply. Line 1 — TW-EF-H36-L1 — XIANG-U-36-02 — Record 211▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H36-L1 — XIANG-U-36-02 — Record 211

211爻 Historical event German hyperinflation unfolded in Germany, Europe during 1921–1923. After the First World War, Germany faced political upheaval, fiscal deficits, reparations obligations, and a weakened tax base. The mark had already lost value during the war, and postwar financing pressures continued to undermine confidence. In 1923, after France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr, the German government supported passive resistance and continued paying workers while production was disrupted. Money creation accelerated as the exchange rate collapsed. Prices began rising so quickly that wages and cash balances lost purchasing power within days or hours. The crisis darkened ordinary economic calculation. Prices no longer served as reliable guides across time, contracts became difficult to write, and households rushed to convert money into goods or foreign currency before purchasing power disappeared. The government ended passive resistance and introduced the Rentenmark in late 1923, alongside fiscal and monetary stabilization. Hyperinflation stopped, though the distributional damage was severe: holders of cash and fixed-income claims were devastated, while some debtors benefited from repayment in depreciated currency. Germany later faced different economic crises, including the Depression. The hyperinflation of 1923 nevertheless left a deep cultural and political memory of monetary instability and the social damage caused when a currency loses its basic function as a store of value and unit of account. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

216爻 Historical event German hyperinflation unfolded in Germany, Europe during 1921–1923. After the First World War, Germany faced political upheaval, fiscal deficits, reparations obligations, and a weakened tax base. The mark had already lost value during the war, and postwar financing pressures continued to undermine confidence. In 1923, after France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr, the German government supported passive resistance and continued paying workers while production was disrupted. Money creation accelerated as the exchange rate collapsed. Prices began rising so quickly that wages and cash balances lost purchasing power within days or hours. The crisis darkened ordinary economic calculation. Prices no longer served as reliable guides across time, contracts became difficult to write, and households rushed to convert money into goods or foreign currency before purchasing power disappeared. The government ended passive resistance and introduced the Rentenmark in late 1923, alongside fiscal and monetary stabilization. Hyperinflation stopped, though the distributional damage was severe: holders of cash and fixed-income claims were devastated, while some debtors benefited from repayment in depreciated currency. Germany later faced different economic crises, including the Depression. The hyperinflation of 1923 nevertheless left a deep cultural and political memory of monetary instability and the social damage caused when a currency loses its basic function as a store of value and unit of account. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. 217爻 Historical event Building societies and household home finance unfolded in Britain, Europe during 18th–20th century. Urbanization created a growing demand for ways that ordinary households could save toward home ownership. Traditional mortgage finance was limited, and many families lacked access to large lump sums. Building societies emerged as mutual organizations in which members pooled regular savings and funds were lent to members for house purchase. Early “terminating” societies dissolved after all members had obtained homes; later permanent societies accepted ongoing deposits and made continuing mortgage loans. The household model linked two sides of personal finance: savers supplied relatively stable funds, and borrowers repaid long-term mortgages. Mutual governance attempted to align the institution with member needs rather than outside shareholders. By the twentieth century, building societies had become major providers of British household savings accounts and mortgages. Financial deregulation and competition later changed the sector, and some large societies converted into banks while others retained mutual ownership. The history of building societies shows how family finance can be institutionalized through repetitive contributions, underwriting, and long repayment schedules. Home ownership was not created by a single payment but by systems that translated household income over time into durable property claims. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. Line 1 — TW-EF-H38-L1 — XIANG-U-38-02 — Record 223▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H38-L1 — XIANG-U-38-02 — Record 223

223爻 Historical event The Homestead labor conflict and industrial wages unfolded in Pennsylvania, United States during 1892. Large U.S. steel companies expanded rapidly in the late nineteenth century, while skilled workers organized to protect wages and workplace authority. At Carnegie Steel’s Homestead plant, management sought lower labor costs and greater control as a union contract approached expiration. Negotiations between the company and the Amalgamated Association broke down. Management locked out workers and hired Pinkerton agents to secure the plant. A violent confrontation followed, and the governor of Pennsylvania sent the state militia. The plant reopened with replacement workers. The dispute was economic as well as political: both sides contested how productivity gains, wage costs, and control over production should be divided. The failure of bargaining turned a contractual disagreement into a broader struggle over power. The union was defeated at Homestead, weakening organized labor in the steel industry for years. Carnegie Steel continued to expand, and the episode became a symbol of the conflict between industrial capital, managerial authority, and workers’ bargaining power. Later labor law in the United States developed very different procedures for collective bargaining. Homestead remains a reminder that groups can share an interest in a functioning enterprise while still oppose one another sharply over distribution and governance. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

226爻 Historical event The Homestead labor conflict and industrial wages unfolded in Pennsylvania, United States during 1892. Large U.S. steel companies expanded rapidly in the late nineteenth century, while skilled workers organized to protect wages and workplace authority. At Carnegie Steel’s Homestead plant, management sought lower labor costs and greater control as a union contract approached expiration. Negotiations between the company and the Amalgamated Association broke down. Management locked out workers and hired Pinkerton agents to secure the plant. A violent confrontation followed, and the governor of Pennsylvania sent the state militia. The plant reopened with replacement workers. The dispute was economic as well as political: both sides contested how productivity gains, wage costs, and control over production should be divided. The failure of bargaining turned a contractual disagreement into a broader struggle over power. The union was defeated at Homestead, weakening organized labor in the steel industry for years. Carnegie Steel continued to expand, and the episode became a symbol of the conflict between industrial capital, managerial authority, and workers’ bargaining power. Later labor law in the United States developed very different procedures for collective bargaining. Homestead remains a reminder that groups can share an interest in a functioning enterprise while still oppose one another sharply over distribution and governance. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

229爻 Historical event 1970s stagflation unfolded in United States / Western Europe during 1970s. Postwar economic policy had been built around an expectation that inflation and unemployment usually moved in opposite directions. By the late 1960s, however, inflationary pressures were already rising in the United States and parts of Europe. The 1973 oil embargo and later energy shocks raised production costs, while wage and price dynamics, fiscal conditions, and monetary policy differed across countries. Many economies experienced the uncomfortable combination of high inflation, weak growth, and elevated unemployment known as stagflation. Stagflation created an obstruction because the standard policy trade-offs seemed unreliable. Stimulating demand could worsen inflation, while tightening policy could deepen unemployment. Energy dependence added a supply-side constraint that domestic demand management alone could not remove. Governments tried combinations of price controls, incomes policies, fiscal measures, and monetary tightening. Results were mixed. By the early 1980s, major central banks placed greater priority on reducing inflation, even at the cost of recession. The experience changed macroeconomic thinking and central-bank practice. It also left businesses and households dealing with uncertain prices, interest rates, and real wages, showing how difficult financial planning becomes when both growth and price stability deteriorate. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line 1 — TW-EF-H40-L1 — XIANG-U-40-02 — Record 235▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H40-L1 — XIANG-U-40-02 — Record 235

235爻 Historical event Volcker disinflation unfolded in United States during 1979–1983. By 1979 U.S. inflation had remained high for years, and repeated efforts to reduce it had not restored confidence in price stability. Expectations of continuing inflation influenced wage contracts, borrowing, and investment decisions. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker led a shift toward tighter monetary policy. Interest rates rose sharply, credit conditions tightened, and the economy entered severe recessions in 1980 and 1981–1982. Unemployment climbed and interest-sensitive sectors such as housing suffered heavily. The policy sought release from an entrenched cycle by accepting near-term pain. Monetary restraint reduced demand and made it more costly to finance price increases, while the persistence of tight policy signaled that the central bank would not quickly reverse course. Inflation fell substantially by the early 1980s. The recovery that followed occurred in an environment of lower inflation expectations, though the distributional and employment costs of the disinflation were large and remain part of the historical debate. The episode reshaped expectations about central-bank credibility and became a reference point whenever later policymakers confronted rising inflation. It demonstrates that escape from a persistent macroeconomic problem can require a clear change of regime rather than incremental adjustments. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line 1 — TW-EF-H41-L1 — XIANG-U-41-02 — Record 241

241爻 Historical event Greek austerity during the euro-area debt crisis unfolded in Greece / Europe during 2010s. Greece entered the global financial crisis with high public debt, persistent deficits, and membership in a currency union that removed the option of devaluing a national currency. In 2009–2010, revised fiscal data and loss of market confidence pushed borrowing costs sharply higher. Greece received financial assistance from European institutions and the IMF in exchange for fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. Taxes rose, public spending and wages were reduced, pensions were changed, and the banking system came under severe pressure as the economy contracted. The crisis centered on “decrease” in a literal fiscal sense, but the economics were difficult: reducing deficits during a recession can shrink demand and tax revenue, while delayed adjustment can worsen debt sustainability and confidence. The distribution of losses also became politically contentious. Public debt was restructured in 2012, additional assistance followed, and Greece eventually exited its main adjustment programs. The economy suffered a deep depression, unemployment surged, and output took many years to recover. The Greek case remains central to debates about austerity, debt relief, and monetary union design. It shows that reducing obligations is not merely an accounting exercise; timing, growth, financing conditions, and social capacity determine whether the reduction stabilizes or further weakens an economy. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944 provided education and training benefits, unemployment support, and federal guarantees for home and business loans. Line 1 — TW-EF-H43-L1 — XIANG-U-43-02 — Record 253▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H43-L1 — XIANG-U-43-02 — Record 253

253爻 Historical event Nixon closes the gold window unfolded in United States / global system during 1971. Under Bretton Woods, the dollar was convertible into gold for foreign monetary authorities at a fixed price, while other major currencies maintained parities against the dollar. By the late 1960s, U.S. inflation, overseas spending, and growing foreign dollar holdings strained the system. On 15 August 1971 President Richard Nixon announced that the United States would suspend dollar convertibility into gold. The package also included a temporary wage-price freeze and import surcharge. Subsequent negotiations produced new exchange rates, but fixed parities did not hold. The announcement was a financial breakthrough in the sense of cutting through an increasingly difficult commitment. It ended one formal promise rather than allowing continuing reserve losses to force the same outcome later under worse conditions. By 1973, major currencies were largely floating against one another. Gold no longer defined the dollar’s international value, yet the dollar retained a central role in reserves, trade, and finance. The change created new exchange-rate risk for businesses and investors and helped reshape global currency markets. It also showed that a decisive policy can solve one constraint while opening a new regime whose risks must then be managed differently. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

259爻 Historical event The 1973 oil shock unfolded in United States / Western Europe during 1973–1974. Industrial economies had become highly dependent on inexpensive oil during the postwar boom. Energy use was deeply embedded in transport, manufacturing, heating, and consumer behavior, while domestic production in some countries could not meet demand. During the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, Arab members of OPEC imposed an oil embargo against selected countries and producers reduced output. World oil prices rose sharply. Governments introduced fuel-saving measures, and businesses faced sudden increases in energy and transport costs. The crisis arrived as an external encounter with a constraint that many economic plans had treated as stable. A commodity whose price had seemed predictable suddenly became a transmission channel from geopolitics into household budgets, corporate margins, and central-bank policy. Inflation accelerated while growth weakened, contributing to recession and stagflation. The shock encouraged energy conservation, new oil production outside the Middle East, strategic petroleum reserves, and changes in energy policy in the United States and Europe. The longer-term response reduced some vulnerabilities but did not eliminate oil-price cycles. The episode became a classic example of how a powerful outside price shock can enter an economy quickly and force decisions far beyond the commodity market itself. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. 265爻 Historical event The creation of the New York Stock Exchange organization unfolded in New York, United States during 1817. New York securities brokers had traded under informal agreements since the 1790s, but the expanding U.S. economy created demand for clearer procedures, regular auctions, and a more organized marketplace. In 1817 brokers adopted a formal constitution and created the New York Stock & Exchange Board, the institutional predecessor of the NYSE. Membership rules, meeting procedures, and trading practices gave buyers and sellers a more structured place to gather. The economic advantage of gathering is liquidity: when more credible buyers and sellers meet in the same venue, it becomes easier to find a counterparty and observe a market price. The exchange also concentrated governance power over who could trade and under what terms. Over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the exchange grew with U.S. railroads, industry, and corporate finance. Technology transformed trading from a physical floor into an electronic marketplace, while federal regulation reshaped listing and conduct rules. The institution’s history shows that a marketplace is not only a location. It is a set of rules that gathers information, capital, intermediaries, and enforcement into a repeatable process, allowing scattered savings to connect with enterprises seeking funds. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

268爻 Historical event The creation of the New York Stock Exchange organization unfolded in New York, United States during 1817. New York securities brokers had traded under informal agreements since the 1790s, but the expanding U.S. economy created demand for clearer procedures, regular auctions, and a more organized marketplace. In 1817 brokers adopted a formal constitution and created the New York Stock & Exchange Board, the institutional predecessor of the NYSE. Membership rules, meeting procedures, and trading practices gave buyers and sellers a more structured place to gather. The economic advantage of gathering is liquidity: when more credible buyers and sellers meet in the same venue, it becomes easier to find a counterparty and observe a market price. The exchange also concentrated governance power over who could trade and under what terms. Over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the exchange grew with U.S. railroads, industry, and corporate finance. Technology transformed trading from a physical floor into an electronic marketplace, while federal regulation reshaped listing and conduct rules. The institution’s history shows that a marketplace is not only a location. 271爻 Historical event The transcontinental railroad unfolded in United States during 1862–1869. The United States had vast distances between its eastern population centers and the Pacific coast. Wagon travel was slow and risky, and political leaders wanted faster movement of mail, passengers, goods, and military resources across the continent. Congress authorized the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads and supported construction with land grants and government bonds tied to completed track. Thousands of workers, including many Chinese laborers in the West, built across mountains, plains, and deserts. The financial structure used public incentives to push private corporations upward through a costly infrastructure challenge. Bonds and land grants reduced financing constraints, while expected future traffic and land values provided private incentives to complete the route. The lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, in May 1869. Travel times fell dramatically, national markets integrated more closely, and towns and industries grew along rail routes. The project also accelerated the dispossession of Native peoples and transformed western ecosystems. Railroads later faced competition, regulation, bankruptcy, and consolidation, but the first transcontinental link permanently changed U.S. economic geography. It demonstrated how long-horizon capital expenditure can raise the scale at which markets operate. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line 1 — TW-EF-H47-L1 — XIANG-U-47-02 — Record 277

277爻 Historical event The Irish Great Famine economy unfolded in Ireland / Britain, Europe during 1845–1852. A large share of Ireland’s poor rural population depended heavily on the potato for food, while landholding and tenancy structures left many households with little resilience. In 1845 potato blight destroyed much of the crop and returned in later years. Food continued to be produced and traded, but many people lacked purchasing power or secure access to enough food. British relief policies changed repeatedly, including public works, soup kitchens, and reliance on the Poor Law, while evictions and disease intensified suffering. The economic oppression came from the interaction of crop failure with poverty, property arrangements, public policy, and market access. Availability of food in aggregate did not guarantee that vulnerable households could obtain it when income and employment collapsed. About one million people died and roughly another million emigrated during the famine years, though estimates vary. Ireland’s population fell dramatically and continued to decline for decades, reshaping labor, landholding, migration, and politics. The famine left a profound demographic and political legacy in Ireland and in emigrant communities, especially in the United States. Its history demonstrates that economic hardship becomes catastrophic when households lose both resources and institutional means of relief. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line 1 — TW-EF-H48-L1 — XIANG-U-48-02 — Record 283

283爻 Historical event London water and sewer infrastructure finance unfolded in London, Britain during 19th century. Rapid nineteenth-century population growth left London with inadequate sewers and heavily polluted water. Repeated cholera outbreaks and the “Great Stink” of 1858 made the health and economic costs of poor urban infrastructure impossible to ignore. Parliament gave the Metropolitan Board of Works authority to build a large sewer network under engineer Joseph Bazalgette. The project used public borrowing and local revenues to finance intercepting sewers, pumping stations, and embankments that redirected waste away from central London. Like a well, urban infrastructure creates a shared service used repeatedly by people who may never see the underlying asset. Long-lived public works require large upfront capital expenditure, debt service, maintenance, and institutions capable of collecting revenue over time. The new system greatly improved sanitation and helped reduce waterborne disease when combined with cleaner water supplies and later public-health improvements. The infrastructure also supported further urban growth and remained in use, with later expansions, for generations. London’s sewer system became a classic example of infrastructure whose value is distributed across public health, property, commerce, and daily life. It shows why some assets are most useful when they are treated as enduring common systems rather than one-time projects. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure. By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

288爻 Historical event London water and sewer infrastructure finance unfolded in London, Britain during 19th century. Rapid nineteenth-century population growth left London with inadequate sewers and heavily polluted water. Repeated cholera outbreaks and the “Great Stink” of 1858 made the health and economic costs of poor urban infrastructure impossible to ignore. Parliament gave the Metropolitan Board of Works authority to build a large sewer network under engineer Joseph Bazalgette. The project used public borrowing and local revenues to finance intercepting sewers, pumping stations, and embankments that redirected waste away from central London. Like a well, urban infrastructure creates a shared service used repeatedly by people who may never see the underlying asset. Long-lived public works require large upfront capital expenditure, debt service, maintenance, and institutions capable of collecting revenue over time. The new system greatly improved sanitation and helped reduce waterborne disease when combined with cleaner water supplies and later public-health improvements. The infrastructure also supported further urban growth and remained in use, with later expansions, for generations. London’s sewer system became a classic example of infrastructure whose value is distributed across public health, property, commerce, and daily life. It shows why some assets are most useful when they are treated as enduring common systems rather than one-time projects. 289爻 Historical event London financial “Big Bang” deregulation unfolded in Britain, Europe during 1986. By the early 1980s, the London Stock Exchange still operated with fixed commissions, separation between jobbers and brokers, and ownership restrictions that critics viewed as limiting competition. Technological change and international finance were also altering the economics of securities trading. On 27 October 1986, reforms known as the Big Bang took effect. Fixed commissions ended, traditional role separations were removed, and outside firms could acquire exchange members. Electronic screen-based trading quickly replaced much of the old floor culture. The reforms were revolutionary because they changed market structure, not merely a few prices. They altered who could own intermediaries, how they charged clients, and how orders were executed, making technology and global capital more important to competitive advantage. Large British and foreign financial institutions expanded in London, and the City strengthened its role as an international financial center. Competition increased, but so did consolidation and the scale and complexity of financial firms. Later financial crises brought new regulation, showing that liberalization does not end the need for oversight. The Big Bang remains a clear case of a financial system deliberately replacing inherited rules when policymakers judged that the old structure no longer matched the market. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

295爻 Historical event Silicon Valley venture-capital ecosystem unfolded in California, United States during 1950s onward. Postwar California combined defense research, universities, semiconductor innovation, skilled engineers, and a culture of new-firm formation. Young technology companies often needed capital before they had stable profits or assets that could secure conventional bank loans. Specialized venture-capital partnerships developed to provide equity financing in exchange for ownership stakes. Investors staged funding over rounds, joined boards, recruited managers, and expected that a small number of successful companies could offset many failures. The “cauldron” was the ecosystem rather than one firm. Technical knowledge, labor mobility, risk capital, stock options, and exit markets combined to turn uncertain ideas into companies capable of scaling quickly when a product found demand. The model helped finance companies in semiconductors, computers, software, biotechnology, and the internet. It spread to other U.S. regions and Europe, though Silicon Valley retained a dense concentration of investors, founders, employees, lawyers, and service providers. Venture capital also encouraged boom-and-bust cycles and can push firms toward rapid growth before sustainable economics are proven. Its historical importance lies in creating a repeatable institutional recipe for financing projects that banks often consider too uncertain. Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. 301爻 Historical event Black Monday market shock unfolded in United States / Europe during 1987. The mid-1980s equity boom had lifted valuations while computer-assisted trading and index futures created new links between cash and derivatives markets. Investors also worried about interest rates, currency tensions, and U.S. trade deficits.

On Monday, 19 October 1987, stock markets around the world plunged. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6 percent, while European and Asian markets also suffered extraordinary declines. Trading systems struggled with order volume and price delays.

The shock traveled through markets faster than many institutions could process information. Selling strategies that appeared reasonable individually interacted with one another, creating feedback at the exact moment liquidity was disappearing.

Central banks emphasized liquidity, exchanges and regulators studied the event, and U.S. markets later adopted coordinated circuit breakers. Despite the severity of the one-day fall, the real economy did not enter a depression comparable to the 1930s.

The event changed operational planning for market stress. It showed that a sudden financial shock can be survivable if payments, funding, and market infrastructure remain functioning, but it also revealed the need to prepare systems for volume far beyond ordinary conditions.

Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

307爻 Historical event Trading halts and market-wide circuit breakers unfolded in United States during 1988 onward. The 1987 crash showed that modern exchanges could experience price moves and order volumes so fast that participants lost confidence in quoted prices and trading systems. Regulators sought mechanisms that could create short pauses during extreme moves.

U.S. exchanges introduced coordinated market-wide circuit breakers, later revised many times. Under current-style systems, specified declines in broad indexes can trigger temporary trading halts, with thresholds and timing rules designed to slow the market during extraordinary volatility.

The economic purpose is to keep still briefly, allowing orders, information, and operational systems to catch up. A halt trades some immediacy for a chance to reduce mechanical disorder, especially when rapid feedback is overwhelming normal price discovery.

Circuit breakers have been activated during later crises, including the market turmoil of March 2020. They do not determine the correct price or prevent losses; after the pause, trading resumes and prices can continue to move.

Debate continues over whether halts calm markets or simply delay trading. Their existence nonetheless reflects an institutional judgment that continuous trading is not always the highest priority when market mechanics themselves are under stress.

Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

309爻 Historical event Trading halts and market-wide circuit breakers unfolded in United States during 1988 onward. The 1987 crash showed that modern exchanges could experience price moves and order volumes so fast that participants lost confidence in quoted prices and trading systems. Regulators sought mechanisms that could create short pauses during extreme moves.

U.S. exchanges introduced coordinated market-wide circuit breakers, later revised many times. Under current-style systems, specified declines in broad indexes can trigger temporary trading halts, with thresholds and timing rules designed to slow the market during extraordinary volatility.

The economic purpose is to keep still briefly, allowing orders, information, and operational systems to catch up. A halt trades some immediacy for a chance to reduce mechanical disorder, especially when rapid feedback is overwhelming normal price discovery.

Circuit breakers have been activated during later crises, including the market turmoil of March 2020. They do not determine the correct price or prevent losses; after the pause, trading resumes and prices can continue to move.

Debate continues over whether halts calm markets or simply delay trading. Their existence nonetheless reflects an institutional judgment that continuous trading is not always the highest priority when market mechanics themselves are under stress.

313爻 Historical event European Single Market unfolded in European Community / European Union during 1986–1993. Postwar European integration had reduced tariffs, but many national rules, technical standards, border procedures, and restrictions on services and capital still divided markets. Businesses faced costs when operating across member states.

The Single European Act of 1986 set a program to complete an internal market by the end of 1992. Hundreds of measures addressed product standards, public procurement, financial services, capital movements, professional rules, and border procedures.

The project was gradual by design. Rather than one treaty instantly creating a unified economy, legal barriers were identified and removed in stages, while common standards and mutual recognition provided ways for national systems to interoperate.

The single market formally began in 1993 and continued to deepen through later legislation and court decisions. It expanded cross-border trade and investment, although national differences and regulatory disputes remained.

The result became one of the world’s largest integrated markets, but it has never been “finished” in every sector. Its history shows how economic integration can advance through many small, coordinated changes whose cumulative effect is larger than any single reform.

Seen as an economic-history episode, the sequence is clear without adding motives that the record cannot establish. The background created a concrete financial or production constraint; institutions and market participants then responded through rules, contracts, investment, borrowing, pricing, or public policy; and the later outcome changed the conditions faced by households, firms, investors, or governments. The case is therefore best read as a chain of observable decisions and consequences rather than as a story of private intentions. Dates, institutional changes, and market outcomes provide the narrative structure.

By the end of the episode, the institutional setting was no longer the same as it had been at the beginning. Rules, financing arrangements, market access, balance sheets, or public expectations had changed in observable ways, and those changes shaped the next phase of economic activity.

Line 1 — TW-EF-H54-L1 — XIANG-L-54-02 — Record 319▶

Line 1 — TW-EF-H54-L1 — XIANG-L-54-02 — Record 319

319爻 Historical event AOL–Time Warner merger unfolded in United States during 2000–2009. At the height of the dot-com boom, America Online had a highly valued internet subscription business and an enormous stock-market capitalization. Time Warner owned major media, publishing, cable, and entertainment assets.

In January 2000 the companies announced a stock merger valued at roughly $165 billion, presenting the deal as a combination of new internet distribution with established content. The transaction closed in 2001, just as the technology market was collapsing and broadband was beginning to weaken AOL’s dial-up model.

The merger joined businesses with very different economics at a moment when one partner’s market valuation reflected exceptional expectations. The legal marriage was completed, but the strategic fit and relative bargaining positions changed soon afterward.

The expected synergies proved difficult to realize. The combined company recorded enormous goodwill impairments, management conflicts became public, and AOL’s importance declined. Time Warner later separated AOL in 2009.
